a: A city designed for people instead of cars would look dramatically different from modern urban environments. Streets would be narrower and more intimate, with wide sidewalks, bike lanes, and green spaces taking precedence over multi-lane roads and parking lots. Buildings would be closer together, creating a more walkable, human-scaled environment where daily necessities are within a short stroll. Car-free zones would be common, with pedestrians, cyclists, and public transit dominating the streets. Parks and plazas would be central features, providing gathering spaces and natural oases. Mixed-use development would be the norm, with homes, shops, offices, and schools integrated into the same neighborhoods. Architecture would be more varied and human-scaled, with buildings rarely exceeding a few stories to maintain a sense of intimacy and connection to the street level. Public squares would replace parking lots, and community gardens would dot the landscape. Transit systems would be frequent, reliable, and accessible, with trams, buses, and bike-sharing stations at every corner. The air would be cleaner, quieter, and more pleasant, with the sounds of conversation and footsteps replacing the rumble of engines. Children would be able to walk to school safely, and elderly residents would have easy access to services and social connections. The overall atmosphere would be more vibrant, social, and connected, with a stronger sense of community and place.
